picks.style: roman drinking-song elegy, plucked lyre and low pipe, rueful tenor, moderate, wry, intimate
picks.why: The bald head as a season: 'dull winter has carried away the bright locks of spring ... a part of thine head hath died already.'

picks.style: rustic latin pastoral, reed pipe and hand drum, plain warm voice, gentle, unhurried, hearthside
picks.why: The poor cottage inventoried — clay cups off a fast wheel, service-berries in wreaths, savory and raisins — all concrete, all singable.

picks.style: sardonic roman cabaret, plucked strings and light percussion, dry mocking baritone, jaunty, clipped, looping
picks.why: 'Whoever has money sails in a fair wind ... Your safe has Jupiter shut up in it' — a complete cynical creed with a punchline.

picks.style: carthaginian lament, frame drum and double reed, wailing female voice, ecstatic, keening, ritual
picks.why: Imilce tearing her hair among the Tyrian mothers, calling her husband home from the wrong war — the poem's one true cry.

picks.style: latin epic conflagration, low brass and crackling percussion, declamatory bass, driving, blazing, relentless
picks.why: The grove burning limb by limb until the bare poplar lets its birds fall from the sky.

picks.style: grim battle chant, war horns and heavy drum, hoarse male voice, hard, unflinching, stamping
picks.why: The severed hand that gropes back to the rein and, knowing nothing, imitates a man still driving.

picks.style: english romantic lyric, acoustic guitar and soft strings, warm tenor, unhurried, wide-open, pastoral
picks.why: 'Tis Distance lends enchantment to the view' — the line the poet is remembered by, sitting in a landscape that opens the song for you.

picks.style: romantic hymn-anthem, chamber organ and swelling strings, soaring soprano, slow, exalted, luminous close
picks.why: The Absalom cry giving way to 'leave — oh! leave — the light of hope behind' — grief and consolation in one arc.

picks.style: scottish border ballad, fiddle and harp, plaintive female voice, strophic, mournful, unhurried
picks.why: Gilderoy's ballad — drum, bell, gallows tree, and the memory of Roslin's glen. Ballad metre, ready to sing.

picks.style: mock greek tragedy, aulos and low drone with frame drum, grave declaiming male voice, slow, portentous, absurdly solemn
picks.why: A tragic curse aimed at gout: nursed in Tartarus by Megaera, milk dripped in by Alecto. Perfect straight-faced parody.

picks.style: greek cult hymn, layered voices over lyre and hand drum, incantatory, building, insistent
picks.why: The litany of epithets — 'who hobble the runner, who rack the ankle-bones, who keep the burning knee awake' — pure singable anaphora.

picks.style: ancient chorus, lyre and frame drum, layered voices, solemn, building, then softening to prayer
picks.why: Salmoneus, Marsyas, Niobe, Arachne — a real tragic ode on mortals who contended with gods, ending in a bargaining prayer to Gout.

picks.style: fairy incantation, harp and small bells with soft frame drum, silvery female voice, quick, conspiratorial, chanting
picks.why: Titania's jealous spell against a marriage — 'Thrice I wave my magic wand' — a charm already written in charm-metre.

picks.style: english ballad lament, acoustic guitar and low strings, tender female vocal, slow, tearful, strophic
picks.why: The strayed child taken in as a broken stem replanted — 'Stay Madelina, child of woe, thy little feet no more shall roam.'

picks.style: moral fable song, harpsichord and viol, clear alto, lilting, trochaic, gently instructive
picks.why: The sun and wind contending for the traveller's cloak, ending on 'Gentleness ... melts the fetters of the mind.'

picks.style: english winter ode, chamber strings and low flute, grave tenor, measured, austere, welcoming the cold
picks.why: 'Winter! art thou welcome to my eye' — the seasons remembered in turn, autumn plucking clusters with a tawny hand.

picks.style: georgian love song, baroque guitar and recorder, warm tenor, lilting, strophic with a returning refrain
picks.why: Lilies, roses, and the refrain 'the kisses are of her I love' coming round twice — a song that already has its hook.

picks.style: bleak pastoral elegy, solo viola and sparse guitar, low voice, slow, wind-blown, desolate
picks.why: 'Where is the spice kiss of the southern gale?' — an ubi sunt for summer, ending alone on a rain-beaten heath with no star.

picks.style: english satirical broadside, fiddle and hurdy-gurdy with tabor, brisk chorus of voices, driving, ironic, relentless
picks.why: The Fable of the Bees in four-beat couplets — envy and vanity as ministers of industry, ending with the poor living better than the rich before.

picks.style: greek bacchic chant, aulos and tambourine, wild high voice, ecstatic, unsettling, quickening
picks.why: The actor playing Agave with the real severed head: 'We bring from the mountain a tendril fresh-cut to the palace, a wonderful prey.'
